newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Liberals face pressure on taxes, jobs.
newsitem.headline: Canada Liberals face pressure on taxes, jobs.

text.p: Canada's high unemployment and taxes will likely top the political agenda as the re-elected Liberals face pressure from a rejuvenated left to create jobs and from the right to cut taxes.

Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals, who won a slim majority in Monday's election, will encounter renewed pressure on the jobs front from a strengthened left-wing New Democratic Party and from leftist Liberal members of Parliament.
Meanwhile the new official opposition -- the right-wing Reform party -- and the Conservative Party, will push their tax cut agenda as Canada's deficit dwindles to zero.
Canada's unemployment rate has been stuck just below 10 percent for months, while Canadians face some of the highest taxation rates in the developed world.
But Chretien took pains to reach out to the left and to impoverished Atlantic Canada on Wednesday.

"We believe that there are still a lot of social and economic problems," Chretien told a news conference. "It was evident (in the election results) that some areas have felt more than others the reality that we had to impose on Canadians."
The Atlantic provinces bruised the Liberals in the election, voting out two cabinet ministers and giving the Liberals only 11 of 32 seats in the region.
Chretien pledged on Wednesday to give the region special attention, saying the next cabinet would examine the area's problems in its first policy meeting next week.
Analysts said the Liberal election platform and Chretien's comments on Wednesday were clear signs the party was prepared to loosen the purse strings.

"There's no question that the government has been moving toward (spending)," said Aron Gampel, economist at Bank of Nova Scotia. "They're going to probably put more money back into the economy in the form of strategic spending priorities in health and education."
But the Liberals appear to have abandoned any direct role for government in creating jobs.
"The reality is that jobs are created by the private sector, no more by the public sector," Chretien said. "My view is that the conditions are there for very good job creation in 1997 and 1998."
He said he expected economic growth of about 3.5 percent this year.
The government did not have much room to manoeuvre if it wanted to keep its popular support, Gampel said.
"The key here is, governments have limited manoeuvring room in today's more fiscally responsible government."
He said the Liberals would likely stay the course on deficit reduction.

In its proudest first-term achievement, the Chretien government slashed the budget deficit from C$42 billion (US$30.5 billion) in 1993 to what was expected to be less than C$16 billion (US$11.6 billion) in fiscal 1996/97 ended March 31.
Chretien repeated on Wednesday that he aimed to balance the country's books within two years.
The new government's job would be made easier by projections of a strong economy, recovering consumer confidence, low inflation and a competitive currency, Gampel said.
The Liberals have promised to spend half of any budget surplus on tax cuts or debt reduction, and the other half on social programmes.
